title: The Qubit and the Bloch Sphere
intro: Every pure state of a qubit, up to global phase, is a point on the unit sphere, and the coordinates of that point are the three expectation values $\langle X\rangle$, $\langle Y\rangle$, $\langle Z\rangle$. This page builds that picture step by step and shows how to read probabilities, overlaps and purity straight off it.

blocks.text: What you need first

Complex numbers in polar form, $z = \vert z\vert e^{i\varphi}$ (Complex Numbers (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers)), kets and inner products (States and Dirac Notation (#/quantum/foundations/states-and-dirac-notation)), and the Born rule (Measurement and the Born Rule (#/quantum/foundations/measurement)). An expectation value $\langle A\rangle = \langle\psi\vert A\vert\psi\rangle$ is the average result of measuring $A$ (Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty)).
What you will be able to do

items: Take any qubit state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$, strip off its global phase, and find its two Bloch angles $\theta$ and $\varphi$.
Compute its Bloch vector $(x, y, z) = (\langle X\rangle, \langle Y\rangle, \langle Z\rangle)$ and check that it has length 1.
Read off the probability of each outcome of a measurement along $x$, $y$ or $z$ (or any axis) straight from the picture.
Tell from the picture whether two states are orthogonal, and compute their overlap from the angle between them.
Explain why the angles in the formula are halved, and what a point inside the sphere means.

blocks.text: How many numbers does a qubit state really need?

A qubit state is written $\vert\psi\rangle = \alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are complex numbers called amplitudes. A complex number is two real numbers (a real part and an imaginary part, or a size and an angle), so on paper a qubit state is four real numbers. That is awkward to picture: four-dimensional spaces do not fit on a page. The good news is that two of those four numbers carry no physical information at all. Once they are removed, two numbers are left, and two numbers can be drawn as a point on the surface of a ball, the way latitude and longitude mark a point on the Earth.

This page does that reduction slowly, because every step of it says something real about quantum mechanics: the first removed number comes from probabilities adding up to one, the second from the fact that an overall phase can never be measured.
Step one: probabilities must add to one
Measuring in the computational basis gives 0 with probability $\vert\alpha\vert^2$ and 1 with probability $\vert\beta\vert^2$. These are the only two outcomes, so

blocks.caption: The normalisation condition. It ties the sizes of the two amplitudes together.

blocks.text: Write each amplitude in polar form, $\alpha = \vert\alpha\vert e^{i\gamma_0}$ and $\beta = \vert\beta\vert e^{i\gamma_1}$. The two sizes $\vert\alpha\vert$ and $\vert\beta\vert$ are two non-negative numbers whose squares add to 1. Any such pair is the cosine and sine of one angle: if $c^2 + s^2 = 1$ with $c, s \ge 0$, there is exactly one angle $a$ between $0$ and $90°$ with $c = \cos a$ and $s = \sin a$. So the two sizes are really one number, an angle. Four real numbers have become three: one angle for the sizes and two phases $\gamma_0, \gamma_1$.
Step two: the global phase cannot be measured

Multiply the whole state by a phase factor $e^{i\gamma}$ (a complex number of size 1). Does anything measurable change? Take any measurement, with any basis state $\vert e\rangle$ as a possible outcome. The Born rule gives

blocks.caption: A phase factor multiplying the whole state drops out of every probability, because |e^{iγ}| = 1.

blocks.text: Every probability, for every possible measurement, is unchanged. Expectation values are built from probabilities, so they are unchanged too. A phase that multiplies the whole state is called a global phase, and $\vert\psi\rangle$ and $e^{i\gamma}\vert\psi\rangle$ are the same physical state. So we are free to choose $\gamma$ to make our life easy. The convenient choice is $\gamma = -\gamma_0$, which makes $\alpha$ real and non-negative. What survives is the difference of the two phases, $\varphi = \gamma_1 - \gamma_0$, called the relative phase.

Global phase and relative phase are different things. A global phase multiplies both amplitudes by the same factor and is invisible. A relative phase changes one amplitude against the other and is very visible: $(\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and $(\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ differ only by a relative phase of $180°$, yet a measurement in the $X$ basis tells them apart with certainty.
Worked example: spotting a global phase
Is $\vert\psi\rangle = (i\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ a new state or an old one in disguise?

items: Step 1. The first amplitude is $i/\sqrt2$. Its phase is $90°$, because $i = e^{i\pi/2}$.
Step 2. Multiply the whole state by $e^{-i\pi/2} = -i$ to make the first amplitude real: $-i\cdot i = 1$ and $-i\cdot(-1) = i$.

Step 3. The result is $(\vert0\rangle + i\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, the state called $\vert{+i}\rangle$. So $\vert\psi\rangle$ is $\vert{+i}\rangle$ with a global phase $i$ in front: the same physical state.

blocks.title: Check yourself: global or relative?
blocks.text: Which of these is the same physical state as $\vert{+}\rangle = (\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$: (a) $(-\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, (b) $(\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, (c) $(e^{i\pi/4}\vert0\rangle + e^{i\pi/4}\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$?
blocks.hint: Ask whether the same factor multiplies both amplitudes.
solution: (a) is $-1$ times $\vert{+}\rangle$, and $-1 = e^{i\pi}$ is a global phase: same state.
(b) changes the sign of only the $\vert1\rangle$ amplitude: a relative phase of $180°$. That is $\vert{-}\rangle$, a different state (orthogonal to $\vert{+}\rangle$ in fact).
(c) multiplies both amplitudes by $e^{i\pi/4}$: a global phase. Same state.

blocks.text: From two numbers to two angles

After the two steps, every qubit state can be written with a real, non-negative first amplitude, a second amplitude whose size is fixed by normalisation, and one relative phase. The standard way to write this uses half-angles:

blocks.caption: The Bloch parametrisation. θ is the polar angle (measured down from the north pole) and φ the azimuthal angle (measured round the equator from the x axis).

blocks.text: Why $\theta/2$ and not $\theta$? Because the size angle $a$ from step one only needs to run from $0$ (all weight on $\vert0\rangle$) to $90°$ (all weight on $\vert1\rangle$). Doubling it, $\theta = 2a$, stretches that range to $0$ to $180°$, which is exactly the range of latitude from the north pole to the south pole. With $\theta$ and $\varphi$ read as the angles of a point on a sphere, every pure qubit state lands on exactly one point of the surface, and (as the next sections show) the coordinates of that point turn out to be the expectation values of the three Pauli observables. That neat fact only works with the half-angles. The price is that angles on the sphere are twice angles between state vectors, which is explained in the section on opposite points.

blocks.alt: A sphere with |0> at the north pole and |1> at the south pole, |+> and |-> on the x axis, |+i> and |-i> on the y axis, and a blue state vector |psi> at polar angle theta from the z axis and azimuth phi from the x axis.
blocks.caption: The Bloch sphere. A pure state is a point on the surface; θ sets the balance between |0⟩ and |1⟩, φ the relative phase.

blocks.text: Worked example: finding the angles
Find $\theta$ and $\varphi$ for $\vert\psi\rangle = \frac{3}{5}\vert0\rangle + \frac{4i}{5}\vert1\rangle$.

items: Step 1. Check normalisation: $\vert3/5\vert^2 + \vert4i/5\vert^2 = 9/25 + 16/25 = 1$. Good.
Step 2. The first amplitude, $3/5$, is already real and positive, so no global phase needs removing.
Step 3. Match the sizes: $\cos(\theta/2) = 3/5 = 0.6$, so $\theta/2 = \arccos 0.6 = 53.13°$ and $\theta = 106.26°$. Check: $\sin(53.13°) = 0.8 = 4/5$, the size of the second amplitude.
Step 4. Match the phase: the second amplitude is $\frac{4}{5}i = \frac45 e^{i\cdot90°}$, so $\varphi = 90°$.
Result: $\theta = 106.26°$, $\varphi = 90°$. The state is a little below the equator (more weight on $\vert1\rangle$ than on $\vert0\rangle$), on the $+y$ side.

blocks.text: Worked example: removing a phase first
Find the angles for $\vert\psi\rangle = \frac{1+i}{2}\vert0\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\vert1\rangle$.

items: Step 1. Sizes: $\vert(1+i)/2\vert = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2}/2 = \sqrt2/2 = 1/\sqrt2$, and $\vert1/\sqrt2\vert = 1/\sqrt2$. Squares add to $1/2 + 1/2 = 1$.
Step 2. The first amplitude has phase $45°$: $(1+i)/2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}e^{i\pi/4}$. Multiply the whole state by $e^{-i\pi/4}$.
Step 3. New amplitudes: $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}e^{-i\pi/4}$.
Step 4. $\cos(\theta/2) = 1/\sqrt2$, so $\theta/2 = 45°$ and $\theta = 90°$: the state is on the equator.
Step 5. The relative phase is $-45°$, which is the same direction as $360° - 45° = 315°$. So $\varphi = 315°$.

blocks.text: At the poles the azimuthal angle means nothing. At $\theta = 0$ the factor $\sin(\theta/2)$ is zero, so $e^{i\varphi}$ multiplies nothing and every $\varphi$ gives $\vert0\rangle$; at $\theta = \pi$, $\cos(\theta/2) = 0$ and every $\varphi$ gives $e^{i\varphi}\vert1\rangle$, which is $\vert1\rangle$ up to a global phase. This is the same as longitude at the North Pole: every longitude meets there.

blocks.title: Check yourself: angles of a state
blocks.text: Find $\theta$ and $\varphi$ for $\sqrt{0.8}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{0.2}\,e^{i\pi/3}\vert1\rangle$.
blocks.hint: Use $\cos(\theta/2) = \vert\alpha\vert$ and read $\varphi$ off the phase of the second amplitude.
solution: The first amplitude is real and positive, so no phase to remove.

blocks.text: Six states worth knowing by heart

Six points of the sphere come up again and again: the two poles and the four points where the $x$ and $y$ axes cross the equator. Each is found by putting a simple $\theta$ and $\varphi$ into the parametrisation. Each point of the sphere also has ordinary Cartesian coordinates $(x, y, z)$, the arrow from the centre to the point; this arrow is called the Bloch vector of the state, and the formulas for it, and what its three numbers mean, come in the next section.

items: North pole, $\theta = 0$: $\vert0\rangle$. Bloch vector $(0, 0, 1)$.
South pole, $\theta = 180°$: $\vert1\rangle$. Bloch vector $(0, 0, -1)$.
$+x$, $\theta = 90°$, $\varphi = 0$: $\vert{+}\rangle = (\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Bloch vector $(1, 0, 0)$.
$-x$, $\theta = 90°$, $\varphi = 180°$: $\vert{-}\rangle = (\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Bloch vector $(-1, 0, 0)$.
$+y$, $\theta = 90°$, $\varphi = 90°$: $\vert{+i}\rangle = (\vert0\rangle + i\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Bloch vector $(0, 1, 0)$.
$-y$, $\theta = 90°$, $\varphi = 270°$: $\vert{-i}\rangle = (\vert0\rangle - i\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Bloch vector $(0, -1, 0)$.

blocks.text: Three operators, the Pauli operators, go with the three axes. On a state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$, $Z$ keeps $\alpha$ and negates $\beta$ (giving $\alpha\vert0\rangle - \beta\vert1\rangle$), $X$ swaps the two amplitudes (giving $\beta\vert0\rangle + \alpha\vert1\rangle$), and $Y$ swaps them and multiplies by phases (giving $-i\beta\vert0\rangle + i\alpha\vert1\rangle$). Each is a measurable quantity with the two possible results $+1$ and $-1$.

Each opposite pair is the pair of eigenstates of one Pauli operator, with eigenvalue $+1$ on the positive axis and $-1$ on the negative one. For example $X$ swaps the two amplitudes, so $X\vert{+}\rangle = (\vert1\rangle + \vert0\rangle)/\sqrt2 = \vert{+}\rangle$ (eigenvalue $+1$) and $X\vert{-}\rangle = (\vert1\rangle - \vert0\rangle)/\sqrt2 = -\vert{-}\rangle$ (eigenvalue $-1$). So the $x$ axis is the axis of the observable $X$, the $y$ axis that of $Y$ and the $z$ axis that of $Z$. Measuring $Z$ asks the state “north pole or south pole?”, measuring $X$ asks “$+x$ or $-x$?”. The Paulis themselves are built up on Pauli Operators and Rotations (#/quantum/qubits/pauli-and-rotations).

blocks.title: Check yourself: place a state
blocks.text: Where on the sphere is $(\vert0\rangle - i\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, and is $(-i\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ the same point?
blocks.hint: Remove any phase on the first amplitude, then read off the relative phase.
solution: Equal sizes, so $\theta = 90°$. The relative phase is that of $-i = e^{-i\pi/2}$, i.e. $\varphi = 270°$: the $-y$ axis.
For the second, remove the phase of the first amplitude by multiplying by $i$: $i\cdot(-i) = 1$ and $i\cdot(-1) = -i$, giving $(\vert0\rangle - i\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ again.
blocks.answer: −y axis (θ = 90°, φ = 270°); yes, the second is the same state

blocks.text: The coordinates are expectation values

So far the sphere is just a drawing aid. What makes it powerful is that the Cartesian coordinates of the point, $x = \sin\theta\cos\varphi$, $y = \sin\theta\sin\varphi$, $z = \cos\theta$ (the usual formulas for a point on a unit sphere), are exactly the average results of measuring $X$, $Y$ and $Z$. Let us derive each one, writing $c = \cos(\theta/2)$ and $s = \sin(\theta/2)$, so $\alpha = c$ and $\beta = e^{i\varphi}s$.
The z coordinate
$Z$ leaves $\vert0\rangle$ alone and flips the sign of $\vert1\rangle$, so its average is (probability of $+1$) minus (probability of $-1$):

blocks.caption: The last step is the double-angle identity cos²a − sin²a = cos 2a.

blocks.text: The x coordinate

$X$ swaps the amplitudes: $X\vert\psi\rangle = \beta\vert0\rangle + \alpha\vert1\rangle$. Taking the inner product with $\langle\psi\vert = \alpha^*\langle0\vert + \beta^*\langle1\vert$ (the bra has complex-conjugated amplitudes) gives

blocks.caption: A number plus its complex conjugate is twice its real part.

blocks.text: With $\alpha = c$ and $\beta = e^{i\varphi}s$, $\alpha^*\beta = cs\,e^{i\varphi}$, whose real part is $cs\cos\varphi$. Since $2cs = 2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2) = \sin\theta$, we get $\langle X\rangle = \sin\theta\cos\varphi$.
The y coordinate
$Y$ sends $\vert0\rangle \to i\vert1\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle \to -i\vert0\rangle$, so $Y\vert\psi\rangle = -i\beta\vert0\rangle + i\alpha\vert1\rangle$. Then

blocks.caption: A number minus its conjugate is 2i times its imaginary part.

blocks.text: The imaginary part of $cs\,e^{i\varphi}$ is $cs\sin\varphi$, so $\langle Y\rangle = \sin\theta\sin\varphi$. Putting the three together:

blocks.caption: The Bloch vector. For a pure state its length is 1.

blocks.text: Its length is 1 for every pure state: $x^2 + y^2 = \sin^2\theta(\cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi) = \sin^2\theta$, and adding $z^2 = \cos^2\theta$ gives 1. This is a real statement about measurements: the three averages $\langle X\rangle$, $\langle Y\rangle$, $\langle Z\rangle$ of a pure state can never all be small at once. If $\langle Z\rangle = 1$ (the state is certainly $\vert0\rangle$), then $\langle X\rangle$ and $\langle Y\rangle$ must both be 0: an $X$ measurement on $\vert0\rangle$ is a fair coin. Being certain about one axis forces complete uncertainty about the others, an uncertainty relation in geometric form.

The formulas $\langle X\rangle = 2\,\mathrm{Re}(\alpha^*\beta)$, $\langle Y\rangle = 2\,\mathrm{Im}(\alpha^*\beta)$, $\langle Z\rangle = \vert\alpha\vert^2 - \vert\beta\vert^2$ work for any normalised amplitudes, global phase or not, because a global phase cancels in $\alpha^*\beta$. Often they are the fastest way to the Bloch vector: no angles needed.
Worked example: a Bloch vector from amplitudes
Find the Bloch vector of $\frac35\vert0\rangle + \frac{4i}{5}\vert1\rangle$ two ways.

items: Step 1 (amplitudes). $\alpha^*\beta = \frac35\cdot\frac{4i}{5} = \frac{12}{25}i$. Real part 0, imaginary part $12/25$.
Step 3 (angles). With $\theta = 106.26°$ and $\varphi = 90°$ from earlier: $x = \sin(106.26°)\cos90° = 0$, $y = \sin(106.26°)\sin 90° = 0.96$, $z = \cos(106.26°) = -0.28$. The two methods agree.

blocks.text: The sample below computes the Bloch vector of the cardinal states and of every worked state on this page, and of the QRC input state used later.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Y = np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1., -1.]).astype(complex)
def bloch(v): return np.real([np.vdot(v, P @ v) for P in (X, Y, Z)])
def state(theta, phi): return np.array([np.cos(theta / 2), np.exp(1j * phi) * np.sin(theta / 2)])
def angles(v):
    v = v * np.exp(-1j * np.angle(v[0])) if abs(v[0]) > 1e-12 else v * np.exp(-1j * np.angle(v[1]))  # remove global phase
    theta = 2 * np.arccos(min(1.0, abs(v[0])))
    phi = np.angle(v[1]) % (2 * np.pi) if abs(v[1]) > 1e-12 else 0.0
    return np.degrees(theta), np.degrees(phi)
for name, (th, ph) in {"|0>": (0, 0), "|1>": (np.pi, 0), "|+>": (np.pi/2, 0), "|+i>": (np.pi/2, np.pi/2),
                       "theta=pi/3, phi=pi/4": (np.pi/3, np.pi/4)}.items():
    r = bloch(state(th, ph))
    print(f"{name:22s} r = ({r[0]:+.3f}, {r[1]:+.3f}, {r[2]:+.3f}), |r| = {np.linalg.norm(r):.3f}")
# Worked states from the page: find the angles and the Bloch vector of any normalised pair of amplitudes
worked = {"(3|0> + 4i|1>)/5": np.array([3, 4j]) / 5,
          "((1+i)/2)|0> + |1>/sqrt2": np.array([(1 + 1j) / 2, 1 / np.sqrt(2)]),
          "sqrt(0.8)|0> + sqrt(0.2) e^{i pi/3}|1>": np.array([np.sqrt(0.8), np.sqrt(0.2) * np.exp(1j * np.pi / 3)]),
          "(|0> + (1+i)|1>)/sqrt3": np.array([1, 1 + 1j]) / np.sqrt(3)}
for name, v in worked.items():
    th, ph = angles(v); r = bloch(v)
    print(f"{name:40s} theta = {th:7.2f} deg, phi = {ph:6.1f} deg, r = ({r[0]:+.3f}, {r[1]:+.3f}, {r[2]:+.3f})")
# Probabilities in three bases for (3|0> + 4i|1>)/5, from the Born rule and from (1 + r.n)/2
v = worked["(3|0> + 4i|1>)/5"]; r = bloch(v)
plus, plusi = np.array([1, 1]) / np.sqrt(2), np.array([1, 1j]) / np.sqrt(2)
print("P(0) =", round(abs(v[0])**2, 4), " (1+z)/2 =", round((1 + r[2]) / 2, 4))
print("P(+) =", round(abs(np.vdot(plus, v))**2, 4), " (1+x)/2 =", round((1 + r[0]) / 2, 4))
print("P(+i) =", round(abs(np.vdot(plusi, v))**2, 4), " (1+y)/2 =", round((1 + r[1]) / 2, 4))
# Antipodal points are orthogonal: the state opposite (|0> + (1+i)|1>)/sqrt3
w = worked["(|0> + (1+i)|1>)/sqrt3"]
th, ph = angles(w); anti = state(np.radians(180 - th), np.radians(ph + 180))
print("antipode amplitudes", np.round(anti, 4), " overlap |<psi|anti>|^2 =", round(abs(np.vdot(w, anti))**2, 12))
# Overlap from geometry: |<a|b>|^2 = (1 + r_a . r_b)/2
a, b = state(0, 0), state(np.pi / 2, 0)
print("|<0|+>|^2 =", round(abs(np.vdot(a, b))**2, 4), " from Bloch vectors:", round((1 + bloch(a) @ bloch(b)) / 2, 4))
# A mixture lies inside the ball: 75% |0>, 25% |+>
r_mix = 0.75 * bloch(state(0, 0)) + 0.25 * bloch(state(np.pi / 2, 0))
print("mixture 0.75|0> + 0.25|+>: r =", np.round(r_mix, 3), " length", round(np.linalg.norm(r_mix), 4))
# The QRC input state sqrt(1-s)|0> + sqrt(s)|1>: Bloch vector (2 sqrt(s(1-s)), 0, 1-2s)
for s in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0):
    r = bloch(np.array([np.sqrt(1 - s), np.sqrt(s)]))
    print(f"s = {s:4.2f}: r = ({r[0]:.3f}, {r[1]:.3f}, {r[2]:+.3f})")

blocks.text: Output of the run: the poles and the equatorial states land on the axes; $\theta = \pi/3$, $\varphi = \pi/4$ gives $(0.612, 0.612, 0.5)$, and every pure state has length 1.000. The worked states come out as $(3\vert0\rangle + 4i\vert1\rangle)/5 \to \theta = 106.26°$, $\varphi = 90°$, $\mathbf r = (0, 0.96, -0.28)$; $\frac{1+i}{2}\vert0\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\vert1\rangle \to \theta = 90°$, $\varphi = 315°$, $\mathbf r = (0.707, -0.707, 0)$; $\sqrt{0.8}\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{0.2}e^{i\pi/3}\vert1\rangle \to \theta = 53.13°$, $\varphi = 60°$, $\mathbf r = (0.4, 0.693, 0.6)$; and $(\vert0\rangle + (1+i)\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt3 \to \theta = 109.47°$, $\varphi = 45°$, $\mathbf r = (0.667, 0.667, -0.333)$. The probability, antipode, overlap and mixture lines are discussed in the sections below; the input encoding gives $(0, 0, 1)$, $(0.866, 0, 0.5)$, $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 0, -1)$ for $s = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1$.

blocks.title: Check yourself: a Bloch vector
blocks.text: Compute the Bloch vector of $\sqrt{0.8}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{0.2}\,e^{i\pi/3}\vert1\rangle$ from the amplitudes.
Reading probabilities off the sphere

Because the coordinates are expectation values of $\pm1$ observables, the probabilities follow at once. If an observable has outcomes $+1$ and $-1$ with probabilities $p$ and $1-p$, its average is $p - (1-p) = 2p - 1$, so $p = (1 + \text{average})/2$. Applied to $Z$:

blocks.caption: The height of the point decides the computational-basis probabilities; the azimuth φ plays no part.

blocks.text: The same reasoning works along any axis. Measuring $X$ gives the outcome $+$ (state $\vert{+}\rangle$) with probability $(1 + x)/2$ and $-$ with probability $(1 - x)/2$; measuring $Y$ gives $+i$ with probability $(1 + y)/2$. For a general axis given by a unit vector $\mathbf n$, the probability of the outcome “along $\mathbf n$” is

blocks.caption: The projection of the Bloch vector on the measurement axis decides the odds.

blocks.text: A useful picture: shine a light along the measurement axis and look at the shadow of the Bloch vector on that axis. The shadow's position, between $-1$ and $+1$, is the average outcome. A vector pointing straight along the axis gives a certain $+$; one at right angles gives a shadow of length 0 and a fair coin; one pointing the other way gives a certain $-$.

Check the $X$ formula directly with the Born rule: $\langle{+}\vert\psi\rangle = (\alpha + \beta)/\sqrt2$, so $P(+) = \vert\alpha + \beta\vert^2/2 = (\vert\alpha\vert^2 + \vert\beta\vert^2 + \alpha^*\beta + \beta^*\alpha)/2 = (1 + x)/2$. The cross term $\alpha^*\beta + \beta^*\alpha$ is exactly $\langle X\rangle$.
Worked example: three measurements of one state
For $\vert\psi\rangle = \frac35\vert0\rangle + \frac{4i}{5}\vert1\rangle$ with Bloch vector $(0, 0.96, -0.28)$:

items: Step 1. $Z$ basis: $P(0) = (1 - 0.28)/2 = 0.36$, which is $\vert3/5\vert^2$, as it should be.
Step 2. $X$ basis: $P(+) = (1 + 0)/2 = 0.5$. The vector is at right angles to the $x$ axis, so an $X$ measurement is a fair coin.
Step 3. $Y$ basis: $P(+i) = (1 + 0.96)/2 = 0.98$. The vector points almost along $+y$.

Step 4. Check step 3 with the Born rule: $\langle{+i}\vert = (\langle0\vert - i\langle1\vert)/\sqrt2$, so $\langle{+i}\vert\psi\rangle = (3/5 - i\cdot4i/5)/\sqrt2 = (3/5 + 4/5)/\sqrt2 = 7/(5\sqrt2)$, and its square is $49/50 = 0.98$. The sample prints the same three numbers.

blocks.title: Check yourself: probability along an axis
blocks.text: A state has Bloch vector $(0.6, 0, 0.8)$. What is the probability of the outcome $+$ when $X$ is measured, and of outcome 1 when $Z$ is measured?
Opposite points are orthogonal states

Two states are orthogonal when $\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle = 0$: a measurement can tell them apart perfectly. On the sphere this has a striking look. Measuring “is the state $\vert\phi\rangle$?” is the same as measuring along the axis $\mathbf r\,'$ of $\vert\phi\rangle$ (the state $\vert\phi\rangle$ is the $+1$ outcome of that measurement). The probability formula of the previous section then gives the overlap of two states directly from their Bloch vectors:

blocks.caption: Θ is the angle between the two Bloch vectors; r·r′ = cos Θ for unit vectors.

items: Same point ($\Theta = 0$): overlap 1, the same state.
Right angles ($\Theta = 90°$), like $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert{+}\rangle$: overlap $1/2$.
Opposite points ($\Theta = 180°$), like $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$ or $\vert{+i}\rangle$ and $\vert{-i}\rangle$: overlap 0, orthogonal.

blocks.text: Now the half-angle makes sense. In the state space, the angle $\Theta_H$ between two unit vectors is defined by $\vert\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle\vert = \cos\Theta_H$. The formula says $\cos\Theta_H = \cos(\Theta/2)$, so $\Theta = 2\Theta_H$: angles on the sphere are double the angles between state vectors. Orthogonal states are $90°$ apart as vectors and so $180°$ apart on the sphere, at opposite ends of a diameter.

A common mistake is to think the opposite of $\vert\psi\rangle$ is $-\vert\psi\rangle$. It is not: $-\vert\psi\rangle$ is the same physical state ($-1$ is a global phase) and sits at the same point. The opposite point is the orthogonal state, which has to be computed: for $\cos\frac\theta2\vert0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac\theta2\vert1\rangle$ it is $\sin\frac\theta2\vert0\rangle - e^{i\varphi}\cos\frac\theta2\vert1\rangle$ (up to a global phase), at polar angle $180° - \theta$ and azimuth $\varphi + 180°$.
Worked example: the antipode of a state
Find the state orthogonal to $\vert\psi\rangle = (\vert0\rangle + (1+i)\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt3$ and check it.

items: Step 1. Normalised? $\vert1\vert^2 + \vert1+i\vert^2 = 1 + 2 = 3$, divided by 3: yes.
Step 2. Angles: $\cos(\theta/2) = 1/\sqrt3 = 0.577$, so $\theta = 2\times54.74° = 109.47°$; the phase of $1 + i$ is $45°$, so $\varphi = 45°$.

Step 4. Check: $\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\cdot\sqrt{\tfrac23} + \frac{1-i}{\sqrt3}\cdot\left(-\frac{1+i}{\sqrt6}\right) = \frac{\sqrt2}{3} - \frac{(1-i)(1+i)}{\sqrt{18}} = \frac{\sqrt2}{3} - \frac{2}{3\sqrt2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{3} - \frac{\sqrt2}{3} = 0$. The sample prints overlap 0.

blocks.title: Check yourself: overlap from the picture
blocks.text: Use the Bloch vectors to find $\vert\langle0\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2$ for the state at $\theta = 120°$ (any $\varphi$). What is the angle between the two state vectors in the state space?
solution: $\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf r\,' = \cos120° = -0.5$, so the overlap is $(1 - 0.5)/2 = 0.25$.
The state-space angle is half the sphere angle: $60°$.

blocks.text: The QRC input state on the sphere

The reset encoding of the Fujii–Nakajima reservoir writes an input number $s\in[0,1]$ into a qubit as $\sqrt{1-s}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt s\,\vert1\rangle$. Its amplitudes are real and non-negative, so $\varphi = 0$: the input moves along the meridian in the $xz$ plane. Using the amplitude formulas, $x = 2\sqrt{1-s}\sqrt s$, $y = 0$ and $z = (1 - s) - s = 1 - 2s$, so the Bloch vector is $(2\sqrt{s(1-s)}, 0, 1 - 2s)$. As $s$ goes from 0 to 1 the point travels from the north pole ($s = 0$) through $\vert{+}\rangle$ ($s = 1/2$) to the south pole ($s = 1$).

Two functions of $s$ appear, one linear ($1 - 2s$) and one with a square root ($2\sqrt{s(1-s)}$). Whatever the reservoir later computes, it starts from these two. That is the nonlinearity budget analysed on Expressivity and Universality (#/qrc/theory/expressivity-and-universality).
Try the sphere yourself

Try this. (1) Drag θ from 0 to 180 and watch $P(1) = \sin^2(\theta/2)$ grow in the bars while the vector travels from the north pole to the south pole. (2) At θ = 90, move φ all the way round: the bars do not move, because $Z$-basis probabilities ignore the azimuth, but the $x$ and $y$ coordinates in the readout trade places. (3) Set θ = 60 and φ = 0: this is exactly the QRC input state for $s = 0.25$, Bloch vector $(0.866, 0, 0.5)$. (4) Set θ = 106 and φ = 90, the nearest whole-degree setting to the worked state $(3\vert0\rangle + 4i\vert1\rangle)/5$ at $\theta = 106.26°$: the readout shows the Bloch vector $(0.000, 0.961, -0.276)$ and $P(0) = 0.362$, within rounding of $(0, 0.96, -0.28)$ and $0.36$.
A first look inside the ball: mixed states

Every pure state sits on the surface. What would a point inside mean? Suppose a machine prepares $\vert0\rangle$ half of the time and $\vert1\rangle$ the other half, at random, and does not tell you which. Averaged over many runs, $\langle Z\rangle = \tfrac12(+1) + \tfrac12(-1) = 0$, and $\langle X\rangle = \tfrac12\cdot0 + \tfrac12\cdot0 = 0$, and likewise $\langle Y\rangle = 0$. Its Bloch vector is $(0, 0, 0)$, the centre of the ball.

Compare with $\vert{+}\rangle$, which also gives $P(0) = P(1) = 1/2$ in the $Z$ basis. But $\vert{+}\rangle$ has $\langle X\rangle = 1$: an $X$ measurement on it is certain. On the random mixture, an $X$ measurement is a fair coin. So the mixture is a genuinely different situation, not a superposition, and it shows up as a point that is not on the surface.

In general a random mixture of states is described by the average of their Bloch vectors, and averaging unit vectors that point in different directions gives a shorter vector. The length $\vert\mathbf r\vert$ measures how pure the state is: 1 on the surface (a pure state), 0 at the centre (the maximally mixed state, total ignorance). The full theory, with density matrices $\rho = (I + xX + yY + zZ)/2$, is on Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states).
Worked example: a mixture

items: Step 1. A source sends $\vert0\rangle$ with probability 0.75 and $\vert{+}\rangle$ with probability 0.25.
Step 3. Length $\sqrt{0.25^2 + 0.75^2} = \sqrt{0.625} = 0.791 < 1$: a mixed state, inside the ball.
Step 4. Probabilities still follow from the coordinates: $P(0) = (1 + 0.75)/2 = 0.875$. Check directly: $0.75\cdot1 + 0.25\cdot0.5 = 0.875$.

blocks.title: Check yourself: pure or mixed?
blocks.text: A state has Bloch vector $(0.3, 0.4, 0)$. Is it pure? What is $P(+)$ for an $X$ measurement?
blocks.hint: Compute the length of the vector.

blocks.text: Putting it together
Take $\vert\psi\rangle = (\vert0\rangle + (1+i)\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt3$. Find its Bloch vector, the probabilities of the three basis measurements, and its overlap with $\vert{+i}\rangle$.

items: Step 1. Amplitudes $\alpha = 1/\sqrt3$, $\beta = (1+i)/\sqrt3$. Then $\alpha^*\beta = (1+i)/3$.
Step 3. Angles: $z = \cos\theta = -1/3$ gives $\theta = 109.47°$; $x = y > 0$ means $\varphi = 45°$.
Step 5. The overlap with $\vert{+i}\rangle$ (Bloch vector $(0, 1, 0)$) is $(1 + \mathbf r\cdot(0,1,0))/2 = (1 + 2/3)/2 = 5/6$, the same as $P(+i)$, as it must be.
Step 6. The orthogonal state is at $\theta = 70.53°$, $\varphi = 225°$, Bloch vector $(-2/3, -2/3, 1/3)$, computed in the antipode example above.

blocks.text: Key points

items: A qubit state has four real parameters; normalisation and the unmeasurable global phase remove two, leaving two angles $\theta$ and $\varphi$.
$\vert\psi\rangle = \cos\frac\theta2\vert0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac\theta2\vert1\rangle$ puts every pure state on the unit sphere.

The Bloch vector is $(\langle X\rangle, \langle Y\rangle, \langle Z\rangle)$; from amplitudes, $x = 2\mathrm{Re}(\alpha^*\beta)$, $y = 2\mathrm{Im}(\alpha^*\beta)$, $z = \vert\alpha\vert^2 - \vert\beta\vert^2$.
The probability of the $+$ outcome along any axis $\mathbf n$ is $(1 + \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf n)/2$.
Overlap is $(1 + \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf r\,')/2$: opposite points are orthogonal; sphere angles are twice state-space angles.
The six cardinal states are the eigenstates of $X$, $Y$ and $Z$.
Mixtures lie inside the ball; the centre is complete ignorance.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Locate a state
blocks.text: Find $\theta$, $\varphi$ and the Bloch vector of $(\vert0\rangle + i\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
blocks.hint: Read $\theta$ from the sizes and $\varphi$ from the phase of the second amplitude.
solution: The first amplitude is real and positive; the second carries $i = e^{i\pi/2}$, so $\varphi = 90°$.
$\mathbf r = (\sin90°\cos90°, \sin90°\sin90°, \cos90°) = (0, 1, 0)$: the $+y$ axis, the state $\vert{+i}\rangle$. From the amplitudes: $\alpha^*\beta = i/2$, so $x = 0$, $y = 1$, $z = 1/2 - 1/2 = 0$.

blocks.title: Angle of an input
blocks.text: What polar angle $\theta$ does the reset encoding $\sqrt{1-s}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt s\,\vert1\rangle$ give for $s = 0.25$? Check the Bloch vector both ways.
solution: $\cos(\theta/2) = \sqrt{0.75} = 0.866$, so $\theta/2 = 30°$ and $\theta = 60°$; the amplitudes are real and positive, so $\varphi = 0$.
From the formulas of the QRC section: $2\sqrt{s(1-s)} = 2\sqrt{0.1875} = 0.866$ and $1 - 2s = 0.5$. They agree.

blocks.title: Overlap from geometry
blocks.text: Use Bloch vectors only (no amplitudes) to find $\vert\langle0\vert{+}\rangle\vert^2$, $\vert\langle0\vert1\rangle\vert^2$ and $\vert\langle{+}\vert{+i}\rangle\vert^2$.
solution: $\vert0\rangle$ is $(0,0,1)$ and $\vert{+}\rangle$ is $(1,0,0)$: dot product 0, overlap $(1+0)/2 = 1/2$.
$\vert1\rangle$ is $(0,0,-1)$: dot product $-1$, overlap $(1-1)/2 = 0$. Opposite points are orthogonal states.
$\vert{+}\rangle$ is $(1,0,0)$ and $\vert{+i}\rangle$ is $(0,1,0)$: dot product 0, overlap $1/2$. Check with amplitudes: $\langle{+}\vert{+i}\rangle = (1 + i)/2$, whose squared size is $2/4 = 1/2$.

blocks.title: Bloch vector of a phased state
blocks.text: Find the Bloch vector of $\frac{1}{2}\vert0\rangle + \frac{\sqrt3}{2}e^{i\pi/4}\vert1\rangle$, and the probability of $+i$ in a $Y$ measurement.
blocks.hint: Same as the $\theta = \pi/3$ example in the sample, but with $\theta = 2\pi/3$.

blocks.title: A state from its statistics
blocks.text: Many copies of a pure state are measured. $Z$ gives 0 with probability 0.9 and $X$ gives $+$ with probability 0.8. The $Y$ data is lost, but you know $\langle Y\rangle \ge 0$. Find the state.
blocks.hint: Turn each probability into a coordinate, then use the length.
solution: A pure state has length 1: $y^2 = 1 - 0.64 - 0.36 = 0$, so $y = 0$.

blocks.text: Where QRC uses this

items: A qubit channel is an affine map of the Bloch ball into itself, the picture used throughout Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels).
Contraction of the Bloch ball is how a reservoir forgets: Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points).
The many-qubit generalisation, the Pauli expansion with $4^n - 1$ coordinates, is the reservoir's full internal state.
